## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">What kind of evidence does an interview produce, and what changes when a model can choose or write the next probe?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 5 generated fixed candidates before participants encountered them. In an adaptive interview, the participant’s answer changes what comes next. The experimental treatment, data-collection instrument and interaction are now entangled.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish interview purposes and survey modes; explain specificity, range, depth and personal context in the focused interview; distinguish speech-to-text, a text interviewer and text-to-speech; compare an assigned protocol with the path a participant actually received; and audit the source and target of every adaptive probe.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Methods:** Merton and Kendall (1946), “The Focused Interview,” *American Journal of Sociology* 51(6): 541–557. Read the complete article. It supplies foundational criteria for evaluating what a probe elicits. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/219886). [@MertonKendall1946]
- **AI interviewing and experimentation:** Velez, Liu and Clifford (2026), “Beyond Belief Change: The Persuasive Returns of Targeting Attitude-Relevant Beliefs,” *American Political Science Review*. Read the complete article. Participants discuss a deeply held issue with an LLM; the model identifies the belief central to their position and generates the personalized treatments used in the experiment. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055426101622). [@VelezLiuClifford2026]
- **Methods and LLMs:** Geiecke and Jaravel (2026), “The Rise of AI-Led Interviews in Social Science.” Read the complete paper. It presents a large text-and-voice implementation and explicit validation exercises. [Paper](https://benjamin.geiecke.com/files/ai_interviews.pdf). [@GeieckeJaravel2026]
- **Substantive application:** Rivera (2012), “Hiring as Cultural Matching,” *American Sociological Review* 77(6): 999–1022. Read the complete article. Rivera uses interviews and observation to show how evaluators construct cultural fit in elite hiring; it gives us a real case against which to assess adaptive probes. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122412463213). [@Rivera2012]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **For a qualitative chatbot case:** Jack, Cooper and Flower (2026), *Methodological Innovations*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/20597991261448157). [@JackCooperFlower2026]
- **For adaptation across respondents:** Velez (2025), “Crowdsourced Adaptive Surveys,” *Political Analysis* 33(4): 284–297. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2024.34). [@Velez2025]

## Sociological and methodological background

Interviews have never been neutral containers into which respondents deposit attitudes. Merton and Kendall’s focused interview began with a situation the researcher had already analysed and used follow-up questions to recover specificity, range, depth and personal context. A good probe could pursue an unexpected response without telling the respondent what that response ought to mean. Later feminist and reflexive work made power, reciprocity and the interviewer’s social position part of the method. These traditions remind us that the interviewer helps produce the account recorded in the transcript.

Rivera’s study makes the evidentiary stakes concrete. Interviewers described cultural fit, while observation showed how evaluators converted shared tastes and experiences into judgments about candidates. The two sources do not simply duplicate one another. An adaptive interviewer might elicit a specific evaluative episode, but a leading probe could also supply the very explanation the study is meant to discover.

Survey researchers approached interviewing with a different priority: administering comparable questions to many people. CAPI placed the questionnaire on an interviewer’s computer; CASI allowed respondents to answer on screen; audio-CASI read recorded questions aloud. Computerized branching could alter what came next, but researchers usually wrote those branches before fieldwork. Velez’s earlier crowdsourced adaptive survey moved adaptation across respondents by allowing their contributions and ratings to change a shared item bank.

Velez, Liu and Clifford move the model inside both the interview and the experiment. A participant identifies a deeply held issue and then discusses the reasons for that position in a semi-structured LLM conversation. The model converts the exchange into an elicited attitude and a *focal belief*: the justification it treats as central to that participant’s view. It also constructs a relevant but previously unmentioned *distal belief*. The participant can then be randomized to a counterargument targeting the focal belief, the distal belief or a placebo topic.

The design joins two methodological problems. First, the interview must elicit a participant’s reasons without supplying them. Second, the model’s interpretation of that interview determines the content of a later experimental treatment. Any error made while probing or summarizing can therefore become part of the intervention.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Velez, Liu and Clifford provide a particularly useful design because the model performs several different jobs. GPT-4o-mini conducts the semi-structured conversation and extracts the participant’s position and focal belief. The system generates a distal belief that bears on the same issue but did not appear in the conversation. GPT-4o then produces the counterarguments. Random assignment identifies the effects of receiving those different messages, but it does not by itself validate the interview, the extracted belief or the semantic equivalence of the generated treatments.

Across two online studies, counterarguments reduced the strength of the beliefs they targeted, with effects still visible roughly ten days later. Counterarguments addressing focal beliefs generally produced larger and more durable changes in the associated attitudes than counterarguments addressing distal beliefs. This makes the quality of the earlier conversation substantively important: the experiment works differently depending on what the model identifies as central to the participant’s position.

Geiecke and Jaravel examine AI-led interviews at larger scale and through both text and voice. Their voice route adds speech-to-text before the language model and text-to-speech after it. Jack and colleagues study a web chatbot and the researchers’ experience of using it. These systems require more than a transcript as a research record. We need the conversation available to the model, each generated probe, the model and prompt settings, and any human edit or approval.

The validation questions now run through the complete chain. Did the probe elicit the participant’s reasoning without suggesting it? Does the focal-belief statement faithfully summarize the exchange? Does the distal belief provide a credible comparison? Do the generated counterarguments differ primarily in what they target? In the Rivera worked example, the first check remains concrete: does the model ask the evaluator to describe a hiring decision, or does it prematurely name “cultural fit” as the cause?

Infrastructure remains part of the method. Audio may pass through a transcription service, while transcripts and prompts may be sent to a model provider. Researchers need to specify which service receives which data, how long those data are retained, who can access the transcript and whether it is reused. Local models can reduce external transfer, but require suitable hardware, model files and maintenance.

## Summary and preparation for next week

An adaptive interviewer produces different question paths from the same protocol. After the midterm break, Week 7 moves from asking people questions to asking a model to answer as if it were a person.
